title: What Makes Some People Uncoachable
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Continuing directly from the prior day's piece on uncoachable traits, this article shifts focus from what can't be coached to who is hardest to coach, and why. It contrasts a growth-mindset orientation (Carol Dweck's term) that makes some people receptive to feedback with several distinct roots of defensiveness in others: excessive self-satisfaction with existing success, perceived expertise, low self-awareness, and deep pessimism about the value of the advice itself. Rather than treating uncoachability as a fixed trait, the piece advises leaders to name the resistance directly and explore its specific root cause with the person, arguing that this conversation itself often loosens the defensiveness. It closes on the idea that no one should be exempt from the expectation that learning is essential.
points: The essay catalogs four distinct roots of coaching resistance (over-satisfaction with success, perceived expertise, low self-awareness, pessimism) rather than treating 'uncoachable' as a single undifferentiated trait.
It borrows Carol Dweck's growth-mindset/fixed-mindset framework explicitly to explain why some people are receptive to feedback and others aren't.
Its key intervention is conversational: naming the resistance and asking about its source directly, rather than working around it silently.
It links back explicitly to the previous day's piece, suggesting the two are meant to be read as a paired argument about coachability.
quotes: What wasn’t mentioned is the idea that some people are uncoachable or at least less coachable than others.

A strong desire to improve sets coachable team members apart. Those who strive to get better are generally more open to feedback and criticism, more vulnerable in their knowledge, and more trusting of learning through others.
They possess what psychologist Carol Dweck calls a “growth mindset” as opposed to a “fixed mindset.
Perhaps the most deceptively simple reason others are defensive and resistant to change is the fact that they like themselves and their outcomes too much.
Instead of accepting this state of affairs, they call out the fact that the other party is resistant to coaching and explore with them their particular reason why.
